client: I've been having a really rough week, honestly. I started this new job a couple months ago and I thought I was getting the hang of it, but then last week in a team meeting my colleague basically called out my mistakes in front of everyone, and I haven't been able to stop thinking about it since. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a try.
therapist: Thank you for giving this a try — it takes courage to reach out, especially when you're not sure it'll help. What happened in that meeting sounds really painful, being put on the spot in front of your team can leave a lasting sting, and it makes sense that it's been hard to shake. I'm curious — when you replay that moment in your mind, what's the thought that tends to come up most strongly for you?

client: Yeah, the thought that keeps coming back is basically... "Everyone in that room now thinks I'm incompetent." Like, I can see their faces in my head, and I just assume they're all thinking the same thing — that I don't know what I'm doing. And then I start to wonder if maybe they're right, which is the part that really gets to me.
therapist: That thought — "everyone thinks I'm incompetent" — is such a heavy one to carry, and the fact that it's turning inward into self-doubt makes it even more exhausting. In CBT, we'd call this a kind of mind-reading, where your mind fills in what others are thinking with the most painful possible version. I'm wondering — if you think about the people in that room, do you have any actual evidence about what they thought, or is your mind mostly filling in the blanks?

client: I mean... I guess I don't have direct evidence, no. But it's not like it came out of nowhere — my manager did cut me off mid-sentence during the presentation, and a couple of people were on their phones the whole time. That feels like more than just my mind making things up, you know?
therapist: You're right to push back on that — those things really did happen, and it's important we don't dismiss them. But I'm curious whether there might be other explanations for them, like a manager who interrupts out of habit, or colleagues distracted by something unrelated to you. What do you think it would mean *even if* some people did notice the mistakes — does that automatically confirm the thought that you're incompetent?

client: I hear what you're saying, and yeah, maybe my manager does interrupt everyone — I honestly haven't paid attention to whether it's just me. But even if that's true, it doesn't really make me feel better, because I *know* I've made real mistakes at work, and I can't just explain those away. Like, if people noticed them, doesn't that mean they're already forming an opinion about me, even if "incompetent" is too strong a word?
therapist: It sounds like you're moving toward something more honest and grounded — acknowledging real mistakes while questioning whether they tell the whole story about you. There's an important difference between "I've made some mistakes while learning a new job" and "people have formed a fixed opinion that I'm incompetent," and it's worth sitting with that distinction. What do you think it would take for someone watching you at work to update their opinion of you — do you believe that's even possible in your mind right now?

client: I mean... I guess logically I know people can change their opinions, but honestly, when I think about my actual workplace, it feels pretty fixed. Like, there's this one colleague who I caught giving me this look after I made that error in the meeting, and now every time I walk past her desk I feel my stomach drop. I want to believe it's possible, but I'm not sure I trust that enough to actually act differently around them.
therapist: That moment with your colleague — the look, the stomach drop every time you pass her desk — shows how much this one event has started to shape how you move through your whole workplace, almost like you're bracing for confirmation of your worst fear. It makes sense that it's hard to act differently when your body is already on high alert, expecting the worst. I'm wondering — what would "acting differently" even look like to you, and what do you imagine might happen if you tried it?

client: Honestly, I think "acting differently" would mean just... walking past her desk without speeding up or staring at the floor, maybe even saying good morning like I used to. But even picturing that makes my chest tighten, because what if she just gives me that cold look again, or worse, ignores me completely? I feel like I'd be setting myself up to get hurt, and I'm not sure I have the energy for that right now.
therapist: It makes a lot of sense that even imagining that small step feels risky — you're already carrying so much from this week, and the idea of reaching out only to be met with coldness feels like it could confirm everything you're afraid of. But I want to gently notice something: right now, avoiding her desk is protecting you from *possible* hurt, but it's also quietly reinforcing the story that there's something to be afraid of. What do you think that daily avoidance is costing you, even if it feels safer in the moment?

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly, part of me knows you're right. The avoidance does cost me something — I spend half my morning just mentally mapping out how to get to the kitchen without passing her desk, and by the time I sit down to work I'm already exhausted and on edge. But I guess I keep telling myself that the cost of avoiding is still less than the cost of actually trying and having her look through me like I'm not even there.
therapist: The fact that you can see this so clearly — the mental mapping, arriving at work already drained before the day even starts — shows real self-awareness, and that matters. What strikes me is that you're already paying a high cost every single day, whereas the thing you're afraid of is still just a possibility. I'm curious — has she actually looked through you like that yet, or is that a moment you're bracing for that hasn't happened?

client: That's... actually a fair point, and it kind of stops me in my tracks a little. She hasn't done it yet, not in the way I'm dreading — but I feel like I'm living inside that moment already, like it's already happened somehow. I guess I've been so convinced it's coming that I've been treating it as a fact instead of a fear.
therapist: That insight you just had is genuinely significant — recognising that you've been living inside a feared future as if it were already real is exactly the kind of shift that can start to loosen its grip on you. There's even something a little relieving in what you said, like a small exhale after holding your breath for a long time. I'm wondering — now that you can see it as a fear rather than a fact, does that change anything about how you want to approach tomorrow morning?

client: I mean... yeah, there is something slightly different about how it feels when I say it out loud like that — like maybe I've been rehearsing a disaster that hasn't actually happened yet. But I'm not sure that changes tomorrow morning all that much, because even if I know it's "just a fear," my chest still tightens the moment I think about walking into that office and facing my colleagues after the way that meeting went. It's like my body hasn't gotten the memo that my brain just had.
therapist: What you're describing — your mind shifting but your body still bracing — is completely normal, and it's actually one of the most important things to understand about anxiety: insight doesn't automatically rewire our physical reactions, and that's not a failure on your part. The good news is that the body *does* catch up, but usually through small, repeated experiences that gently teach it the disaster didn't come. I'm wondering — given everything we've talked about today, is there one tiny thing, even smaller than saying good morning, that might feel like a manageable first step tomorrow?

client: I hear what you're saying, and it actually does help a little to know my body isn't just broken or something. But I'm sitting here trying to think of something even smaller than saying good morning, and honestly... even making eye contact in the hallway feels like a lot. I guess maybe just not looking away so fast when someone walks by? But I'm already second-guessing it, like what if that makes things more awkward and I end up feeling worse than before.
therapist: Not looking away so fast — that's actually a really meaningful step, and I want you to hold onto the fact that *you* came up with that, not me. It's worth naming that even if it feels awkward in the moment, awkward isn't the same as disaster, and one brief moment of eye contact is also a small piece of evidence your body can start to learn from. What would you tell a close friend who came up with a brave little step like that and then immediately started talking themselves out of it?
